To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
12 Mycobacterial VapCs are endoribonuclease toxins that target the decoding center of the ribosome.
the major human pathogen M. tuberculosis uses a large cohort of VapC toxins to inhibit translation by cleaving RNAs essential for the decoding step at the ribosomal decoding center.
VapCs of M. tuberculosis are endoribonuclease toxins that cleave RNPs essential for decoding at ribosomal A-site.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which Mycobacterium species evade immune surveillance and survive in the host.
the identification of the cellular targets of VapCs from Mycobacterium tubercu-losis and the characterization of their mode of action.
the identification of cellular targets of VapCs of M. tuberculosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the VapCs of M. tuberculosis are all endorribonucleases that target tRNAs and/or 23S rRNAs.
the VapBC modules are not only virulence factors but rather survival factors.
the vapBC genes are a major contributor to the persistence of M. tuberculosis by reducing the level and efficiency of translation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vapBC genes are not just a family, they are a class of toxins that target the ribosome.
M. tuberculosis uses a large cohort of vapBC modules to inhibit the host cell’s protein synthesis machinery, thereby contributing to the organism’s survival in its human host.
the VapCs of M. tuberculosis cleave RNAtargets that are essential for translation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PIN domain endoribonuclease activity is a conserved property of VapC proteins.
the VapC toxin of M. tuberculosis cleaves tRNA rather than rRNA, as is the case for other bacteria.
the vapBC modules in M. tuberculosis have evolved to target different cellular RNA species.
